newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: SWISS SEEK MORE DETAILS ON MOBUTU FUNDS.
newsitem.headline: SWISS SEEK MORE DETAILS ON MOBUTU FUNDS.

text.p: Swiss judicial authorities said on Friday they were writing to the government of newly-installed President Laurent Kabila seeking more details of funds allegedly left by his predecessor Mobutu Sese Seko in this Alpine haven.
Separately, the Swiss Federal Banking Commission said it planned to publish on Tuesday the results of its search for any funds which may have been left behind by the deposed ruler.

The Swiss letter will be sent early next week to Justice Minister Celestin Lwangi, who in an interview with a Geneva daily (Le Nouveau Quotidien) on Thursday alleged Mobutu had stashed 11 billion Swiss francs ($7.3 billion) in Switzerland.

Hours after Mobutu was ousted from power nearly two weeks ago, the Swiss Federal Cabinet froze all bank accounts and other assets he and his family might have in Switzerland, including his huge villa above Lausanne, valued at $5.5 million.

Swiss authorities were acting on a request for judicial assistance in recovering Mobutu funds, filed a week earlier by the public prosecutor of Lumbumbashi who had joined the rebels. But Swiss officials said the request lacked specific details.

"We will send a letter in the diplomatic pouch asking the justice ministry to supply us with necessary supplementary information," Folco Galli of the Swiss Federal Office of Police Matters told Reuters. "The pouch will go early next week."
"In matters of judicial assistance we cannot go on a fishing expedition. We need more precise information," Galli added.

Meanwhile, the Swiss Federal Banking Commission, which asked 417 banks in the country to report back by May 30 on any Mobutu assets in their coffers, is still awaiting replies from some 75 of them, according to its chairman.
Banking Commission chairman Kurt Hauri declined to reveal whether responses by 342 banks so far had uncovered any Mobutu funds. The Commission would issue a statement on Tuesday.
"The deadline has not passed yet. So far, as of Thursday, 75 of the 417 banks have yet to reply," Hauri told Reuters.

Replies postmarked on Friday and received by Tuesday would be considered as having met the deadline. Based in Berne, the Swiss Federal Banking Commission is an independent surveillance body for banks and stock exchanges.
"We may make a second request, extending the deadline by a very short period of one or two days," Hauri said. "We won't remain idle."
"Our only aim is to establish the facts. If ever assets are found, they are already blocked and their fate is to be determined by the government and tribunals," Hauri added.

But Swiss bankers -- tarnished by scandals over the Swiss assets of former Philippine leader Ferdinand Marcos and Haiti's Jean-Claude Duvalier -- are sceptical that their wary institutions would have accepted Mobutu funds.
Many Swiss lawyers with expertise in international requests for legal assistance in criminal matters also doubt that significant Mobutu funds would be identified in Switzerland.
Furthermore, under Swiss law, the new government of the Democratic Republic of the Congo would have to file criminal proceedings at home against Mobutu in order to have a case.
"It is just paperwork, maybe even a paperchase," said one Swiss lawyer who asked not to be named.
